screens.title: Cloud Security: Shared Responsibility Model
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson introduces the shared responsibility model, the foundational idea that the cloud provider secures the platform and the customer secures what they put inside it. You will learn a precise distinction: security of the cloud versus security in the cloud, and how that boundary shifts across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. Understanding this model prevents a common class of cloud breaches caused by mistaken assumptions about who is responsible for patching, access control, and configuration. We will walk through concrete examples you will encounter in enterprise environments: an unpatched virtual machine, a publicly writable storage bucket, and weak account configuration in a SaaS application. For each, you will learn which party holds primary responsibility and what customer-side controls would have prevented the incident. By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain to stakeholders which controls you must own, how to verify them, and where to perform vendor due diligence. Think of this as the governance rulebook for cloud deployments: know what the CSP maintains, and own the rest. How will you change your checklist after seeing one real misconfiguration?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Cloud Security Model
Cloud Security: Shared Responsibility
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Learn the operational boundary between what a Cloud Service Provider secures and what you must secure within cloud services. This orientation reduces misconfiguration risk and supports auditability.

Security of the cloud

Physical facilities, host infrastructure, hypervisor, and service availability—managed by the CSP.

Security in the cloud

Your data, OS patching, application hardening, IAM, and configuration are your responsibility.

In this lesson
Real examples, model boundaries, and common pitfalls

We will analyze S3 misconfiguration and an unpatched VM to show where customers must act.

Explore Key Topics
IaaS Responsibilities

OS patching, security groups, application hardening.

PaaS & App Config

Platform-managed OS, customer-managed code and platform settings.

SaaS Controls

User accounts, MFA, data governance inside the application.

Concept Map
Security of the Cloud
CSP: data centers, hypervisors, networking, service code.
Security in the Cloud
Customer: OS, apps, data, network configuration, IAM.
Service Models
IaaS, PaaS, SaaS — responsibilities shift as you move up the stack.
Key Takeaway

Always confirm the provider's shared responsibility matrix for the services you use, and own patching, access control, and data governance for resources you deploy.

screens.title: Defining 'Security of' vs 'Security in' the Cloud
screens.narratorSegment: Start by defining two related but distinct claims. 'Security of the cloud' is the Cloud Service Provider's responsibility to protect the infrastructure that runs cloud services. That includes physical data centers, network fabric, storage hardware, and the virtualization layer. CSPs invest in environmental controls, physical access restrictions, and maintenance of service code. In contrast, 'security in the cloud' is the customer's responsibility for everything they deploy and manage inside a cloud account: data, applications, operating systems, network configurations, and identity and access management. A concrete example helps: when a provider offers an object storage service, the provider maintains the storage platform and the encryption of data at rest as part of the service offering, but the customer must configure bucket policies and user access so only authorized principals can retrieve objects. A common misconception is to assume that because a service is managed, the provider automatically configures secure defaults for every tenant; this is not true. Many defaults leave options open for flexibility and must be hardened by the customer. Takeaway: use the provider's shared responsibility matrix to decide what you must secure and document that in your control plan.

keyIdea.title: Definition summary
keyIdea.text: 'Security of' = CSP infrastructure; 'Security in' = customer-managed resources and configurations.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Definition
Security of the cloud

The CSP secures physical facilities, host hardware, networking, hypervisor, and service-level controls. This is the provider's operational perimeter to keep the cloud resilient and available.

Examples
Data center physical access controls, hypervisor patching, network isolation between tenants.
Misconception check
Do not assume the provider configures tenant policies for you; those remain your job unless explicitly managed.
Security in the cloud

Customer responsibility for data, OS, applications, network configuration, IAM policies, encryption keys, and logging. These are the controls you must own and operate for your workload.

Concrete example
If an S3 bucket is publicly writable due to bucket policies, the customer is responsible for correcting the policy and auditing permissions.
Key controls
  • OS patching and hardening
  • Application security testing
  • IAM, MFA, and least privilege
  • Encryption and data classification
Key Takeaway

Always read the provider's shared responsibility details for each service you use and treat the 'in cloud' items as your operational controls to manage and prove.

screens.title: What customers must do in IaaS
screens.narratorSegment: In an Infrastructure as a Service deployment the customer holds the largest share of security responsibilities. The provider secures the physical layer, virtualization, and underlying network. Customers are responsible for the virtual machines they launch: the operating system requires regular patching and hardening, host-based anti-malware, and local firewall configuration. Applications deployed on those VMs need secure coding, vulnerability management, and web application firewalls where appropriate. Network configuration is also critical — security groups and network access control lists are virtual boundaries you must define to restrict traffic. Data protection remains your duty: encrypt data at rest and in transit, classify data, and apply data loss prevention where needed. Identity and access management for those resources — user accounts, roles, multi-factor authentication, and least privilege — are customer obligations. A common misstep is assuming the CSP manages VM-level patching; this is false. A concrete example is an unpatched EC2 instance running a vulnerable web app that was compromised; responsibility falls to the customer because they control the OS and application. Closing this gap requires an automated patch management strategy, scheduled scans, and enforcement of secure baseline images. After reviewing responsibilities, ask how you will enforce these controls in your environment.

keyIdea.title: IaaS focus
keyIdea.text: Customer: OS, apps, network rules, data encryption, IAM, and configuration management for their VMs and resources.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › IaaS Responsibilities
Customer-owned controls in IaaS

When you use virtual machines and raw storage, you own the OS, apps, network rules and data protections that run on those resources.

OS & Host
Patching, hardening, host-based firewalls and anti-malware are your responsibility for each VM you deploy.
Network
Security groups, NACLs, VPNs, and subnet design control traffic to and from your instances.
Data & IAM
Encryption, key management, data classification, and user/role permissions are customer duties.
Example scenario

An EC2 instance runs a web app with an unpatched OS. An attacker exploits a known kernel vulnerability and gains control. This is a customer responsibility because the guest OS and application are managed by the customer.

Mitigation
Automate patch management with a systems manager, use hardened baseline images, and run scheduled vulnerability scans.
Common Mistake
Assuming the CSP will patch guest operating systems on your behalf.
Key Takeaway

In IaaS you must operate and verify OS/ application patching, network controls, and data protections for resources you provision.

screens.title: Network and Storage Misconfigurations
screens.narratorSegment: Two of the most frequent customer-side mistakes in IaaS are overly permissive network rules and misconfigured storage permissions. Overly broad security groups, for example allowing SSH from everywhere, immediately expands the attack surface and makes brute-force or automated exploit attempts likely. Similarly, storage buckets with public access can expose sensitive customer data if policies or ACLs are incorrect. A concrete case: an S3 bucket containing customer records became publicly accessible because a bucket policy allowed public read; the provider hosts the S3 infrastructure, but the customer configured the policy that exposed the data. Addressing these mistakes is a process you can operationalize. Step one: inventory all public-facing endpoints and storage; step two: enforce account-level defaults that block public bucket creation; step three: run continuous configuration checks with automated tools and remediate findings. Use least privilege for network rules — only allow source IPs or security groups that require access. Misconceptions include thinking that private VPCs automatically protect all attached storage; storage still needs explicit access controls. Practice: run a configuration audit and ask which rules are justified by business needs.

keyIdea.title: Fix process
keyIdea.text: Inventory, enforce account-level defaults to block risky configs, scan continuously, and remediate automatically.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Process Flow
Remediation process for misconfigurations

Use a repeatable process to detect and remediate security group and storage permission errors before they become breaches.

1. Inventory
List all public endpoints, security groups with broad rules, and public storage objects.
2. Enforce Defaults
Block public bucket policies at account level and establish minimal open security group templates.
3. Continuous Scan
Run automated checks and remediate findings with scripts or a CSPM tool.
Concrete example

An S3 bucket became public because a policy allowed public reads. The correct owner to fix the policy is the customer: they control bucket policies and ACLs. The provider secures the S3 service, but not your bucket policy.

Common Mistake

Believing that storage lives behind the VPC and inherits network protections — storage access is controlled by resource-level policies and must be reviewed.

Key Takeaway

Treat storage and network access as separate control planes and verify both are correctly configured by the customer.

screens.title: Platform as a Service — what shifts to the CSP
screens.narratorSegment: Platform as a Service moves more responsibility to the provider: they manage the operating system, runtime, middleware, and underlying infrastructure. This reduces the customer's duty to patch OS images and manage servers, but it does not remove customer responsibilities entirely. Customers still own application security: secure coding, dependency management, and vulnerability scanning remain critical. Data security is still yours: you must apply encryption, classification, and proper access controls for managed databases or storage. Identity and access management inside the platform must be configured and maintained by the customer, including A P I keys, environment variables, and platform-level roles. A frequent oversight is assuming that because the OS is managed, sensitive data or database users are automatically protected at the application level. For example, a managed database may be patched by the CSP, but you are responsible for strong passwords, least-privilege database users, and encrypting sensitive columns. The right controls combine platform settings and customer-side policies to protect data and access within PaaS offerings. Platform as a Service — what shifts to the CSP means csp manages os/runtime; customer manages app code, database access, data encryption, and iam within the platform.. In practical terms, platform-managed os and runtime, customer-managed code and data.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: PaaS boundary
keyIdea.text: CSP manages OS/runtime; customer manages app code, database access, data encryption, and IAM within the platform.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › PaaS
What the provider manages

In PaaS the CSP handles OS, runtimes, middleware, and the host infrastructure so you don't manage servers directly.

Provider responsibilities
Runtime maintenance, patching of the platform, and infrastructure availability.
Customer responsibilities
  • Application code security and dependency management
  • Database user permissions and sensitive-field encryption
  • Platform configuration such as API keys and environment access
Concrete example

A managed database is patched by the CSP, but the customer must enforce strong passwords, limit users to least privilege, and encrypt sensitive columns to prevent data exposure if credentials are leaked.

Common Mistake

Assuming that platform-level patching removes the need for application-level security controls and key management.

Key Takeaway

PaaS reduces infrastructure chores but requires you to secure code, data access, and platform-specific configurations.

screens.title: SaaS — what remains with the customer
screens.narratorSegment: Software as a Service places the heaviest operational burden on the provider for infrastructure and application maintenance. The CSP manages availability, application patches, server OS, and platform security. Customer responsibilities are narrower but still critical: user identities, access controls, data classification, and application-specific configurations. For instance, migrating email to a SaaS productivity suite makes the provider responsible for service availability and server patching, but the customer must enforce multi-factor authentication, manage user roles, and configure retention and sharing policies for sensitive data. A common pitfall is neglecting strong authentication or granting overly broad permissions inside the SaaS application; a compromised account can still lead to data exfiltration. Data governance remains a customer duty — you must know what data is stored, its sensitivity, and ensure compliance controls like retention and labeling are applied. In short, SaaS reduces infrastructure management but increases the importance of identity controls and data governance inside the application. SaaS — what remains with the customer means csp manages the app stack; customer manages identities, mfa, data classification, governance, and app configuration.. In practical terms, account management, data governance, and configuration inside the application.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: CSP manages the app stack; customer manages identities, MFA, data classification, governance, and app configuration.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › SaaS
Customer duties for SaaS

Your responsibilities typically focus on identities, authentication, data governance, and per-tenant configuration inside the SaaS application.

Identity & Access
Configure MFA, role assignments, and least privilege for all users.
Data Governance
Classify and enforce retention, sharing, and encryption policies for data within the app.
Concrete example

Migrating email to Microsoft 365 means Microsoft maintains servers and patches; you must enforce MFA, configure mailbox permissions, and set retention policies to meet compliance.

Common Mistake

Assuming provider oversight removes the need for strong tenant-level authentication and permission management.

Key Takeaway

Even with SaaS, the customer must own identity hygiene and data governance to prevent account-based breaches.

screens.title: Automated Controls: Patching and Access Blocks
screens.narratorSegment: Automation is a central technique for meeting customer responsibilities at scale. For patch management, use a systems manager to apply OS updates automatically across instances. For storage, block public access by default at the account level and audit for exceptions. The chapter provides concrete command examples you can run or adapt. The first sample shows how to block public access on an S3 bucket using the provider CLI. The second sample shows how to request a patch run via a systems manager command. These are concrete actions you can automate from CI/CD or runbooks. A misconception is thinking manual fixes are sufficient; automation reduces human error and ensures consistency. Use scheduled scans and playbooks to detect deviations and revert insecure configurations automatically. Below are the exact command examples you may reuse when authorized on your accounts. After running them, verify configurations with an inventory tool and log the changes for auditability. keyIdea.title: Automate remediation
keyIdea.text: Use provider automation and account-level policies to block risky defaults and apply patches consistently.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Automation
Block public S3 access (example)

Use account or bucket-level policies to prevent public ACLs and public policies. This command sets the public access block configuration for a bucket.

aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket your-sensitive-data-bucket \
  --public-access-block-configuration "BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true"
Replace the bucket name and run with appropriate credentials. Then verify with an inventory tool or the provider console.
Trigger an OS patch run (example)

Use your provider's systems manager to install patches across instances with a single command.

aws ssm send-command \
  --instance-ids "i-0abcdef1234567890" \
  --document-name "AWS-RunPatchBaseline" \
  --comment "Apply OS patches" \
  --parameters 'Operation=Install'
Schedule this in a maintenance window and track results in the systems manager console. Automate reporting for auditors.
Key Takeaway

Prefer repeatable automation over ad-hoc fixes. Automate blocking of dangerous defaults and scheduled patching to reduce human error.

screens.title: IAM: who controls access in the cloud?
screens.narratorSegment: Identity and Access Management is a continuous customer responsibility across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. You must manage user accounts, enforce strong authentication such as multi-factor authentication, and design role-based or attribute-based access control aligned with least privilege. The model requires you to decide who can create resources, who can modify policies, and who can access sensitive data. Concrete practices include using roles for services instead of long-lived credentials, requiring MFA for administrative actions, and regularly reviewing role permissions. A misconception is that a provider will manage your tenant's user accounts; providers manage infrastructure accounts but not the identities you create for your organization. Audit and logging are essential: retain logs showing who accessed what and when so you can perform forensic analysis and compliance reporting. Example incident

A SaaS administrator account without MFA was phished and used to download sensitive reports. The account had broad export permissions. Responsibility for enforcing MFA and limiting that account's scope rests with the customer.

Mitigation
Require MFA, limit export permissions, and create a delegated role for administrative tasks with session duration limits.
Audit
Enable and retain access logs to track who assumed roles and what actions were performed for forensic analysis and compliance.

Treat IAM as a primary control: enforce MFA, minimize privilege, and log all privileged actions to reduce compromise impact.

screens.title: Data Classification, Logging, and Compliance
screens.narratorSegment: Across service models customers must maintain visibility into their data and controls to meet compliance and audit requirements. Data classification is the first step: know what data you store, its sensitivity, and where it resides. This informs encryption choices, retention policies, and access controls. Logging and audit trails are also customer responsibilities: configure and retain logs that show access to data, configuration changes, and administrative actions. For managed services, ask the provider what logs they produce and what you must capture within your tenant. A common misconception is treating provider-side logs as sufficient; many provider logs show infrastructure events but not tenant-level application accesses. Practical steps include enabling object access logs, centralizing logs in an immutable store, and running regular audits that map controls to regulatory requirements. Incident response plans must include roles, notification paths, and evidence preservation steps. Demonstrating to auditors that you classify data, configure logging, and can produce audit trails proves you are meeting your side of the shared responsibility model. screens.title: Prepare for incidents and evaluate providers

screens.title: Breach Analysis: Apply the shared responsibility model
screens.narratorSegment: Now apply what you've learned to a real scenario. Imagine an AWS IaaS deployment where a breached S3 bucket exposed customer data and an unpatched EC2 instance was compromised. Your task is to identify which aspects of the breach are the provider's responsibility and which are the customer's, then propose mitigations for each customer-side failure. For the S3 bucket, responsibility for the bucket policy and ACLs lies with the customer; AWS provides the S3 service but does not set your bucket policies. The mitigation is to block public access at the account or bucket level and audit bucket policies regularly. For the unpatched EC2 OS, the customer owns patching and application hardening; apply automated patch management and vulnerability scanning. When you write your analysis include justification referencing the shared responsibility model. A common misconception is blaming the CSP for tenant misconfigurations; make your recommendations actionable and owner-specific — this is how you demonstrate control during incident reviews and audits. screens.title: What to Remember — Part 1

fullNarratorScript:
This lesson introduces the shared responsibility model, the foundational idea that the cloud provider secures the platform and the customer secures what they put inside it. You will learn a precise distinction: security of the cloud versus security in the cloud, and how that boundary shifts across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. Understanding this model prevents a common class of cloud breaches caused by mistaken assumptions about who is responsible for patching, access control, and configuration. We will walk through concrete examples you will encounter in enterprise environments: an unpatched virtual machine, a publicly writable storage bucket, and weak account configuration in a SaaS application. For each, you will learn which party holds primary responsibility and what customer-side controls would have prevented the incident. By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain to stakeholders which controls you must own, how to verify them, and where to perform vendor due diligence. Think of this as the governance rulebook for cloud deployments: know what the CSP maintains, and own the rest. How will you change your checklist after seeing one real misconfiguration?

These objectives prepare you to operate as a CASP+ practitioner in cloud environments. First, you will learn to articulate the core principles of the shared responsibility model across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. That means being able to state precisely which layers the CSP protects and which layers you must secure. Second, you will identify specific security responsibilities typically handled by the CSP versus those that remain the customer's. You'll practice mapping tasks like OS patching and bucket access policies to the correct owner. Third, you will analyze how this boundary shifts with service models and vendor offerings, so you can advise architects on risk and control placement. Finally, you will develop practical strategies to ensure customer responsibilities are addressed: IAM hygiene, patch management, configuration audits, and incident response. Each objective connects to a competency milestone so you can demonstrate verification to stakeholders. By the end of these activities you will both explain the model and propose controls that close common gaps. Which objective will you practice first with your team?

This second objectives slide focuses on applied skills and common mistakes to watch for. You will practice auditing configurations — for example, verifying that S3 buckets are not publicly accessible and that security groups are not wide open. You will also learn to design and validate patch management for IaaS virtual machines and to assess managed database access controls in PaaS. A key objective is to identify misconceptions: many teams assume the CSP patches the guest OS or that a managed database removes the need for column-level encryption. You will learn how to challenge those assumptions with evidence from the provider's shared responsibility documentation. Finally, you will build short remediation plans: a set of controls, tools, and verification steps to remediate customer-side failures. These are practical competences you can demonstrate to auditors and leadership, reducing the chance that a misconfiguration becomes a breach. Which misconfiguration will you fix first in your environment?

Start by defining two related but distinct claims. 'Security of the cloud' is the Cloud Service Provider's responsibility to protect the infrastructure that runs cloud services. That includes physical data centers, network fabric, storage hardware, and the virtualization layer. CSPs invest in environmental controls, physical access restrictions, and maintenance of service code. In contrast, 'security in the cloud' is the customer's responsibility for everything they deploy and manage inside a cloud account: data, applications, operating systems, network configurations, and identity and access management. A concrete example helps: when a provider offers an object storage service, the provider maintains the storage platform and the encryption of data at rest as part of the service offering, but the customer must configure bucket policies and user access so only authorized principals can retrieve objects. A common misconception is to assume that because a service is managed, the provider automatically configures secure defaults for every tenant; this is not true. Many defaults leave options open for flexibility and must be hardened by the customer. Takeaway: use the provider's shared responsibility matrix to decide what you must secure and document that in your control plan.

In an Infrastructure as a Service deployment the customer holds the largest share of security responsibilities. The provider secures the physical layer, virtualization, and underlying network. Customers are responsible for the virtual machines they launch: the operating system requires regular patching and hardening, host-based anti-malware, and local firewall configuration. Applications deployed on those VMs need secure coding, vulnerability management, and web application firewalls where appropriate. Network configuration is also critical — security groups and network access control lists are virtual boundaries you must define to restrict traffic. Data protection remains your duty: encrypt data at rest and in transit, classify data, and apply data loss prevention where needed. Identity and access management for those resources — user accounts, roles, multi-factor authentication, and least privilege — are customer obligations. A common misstep is assuming the CSP manages VM-level patching; this is false. A concrete example is an unpatched EC2 instance running a vulnerable web app that was compromised; responsibility falls to the customer because they control the OS and application. Closing this gap requires an automated patch management strategy, scheduled scans, and enforcement of secure baseline images. After reviewing responsibilities, ask how you will enforce these controls in your environment.

Two of the most frequent customer-side mistakes in IaaS are overly permissive network rules and misconfigured storage permissions. Overly broad security groups, for example allowing SSH from everywhere, immediately expands the attack surface and makes brute-force or automated exploit attempts likely. Similarly, storage buckets with public access can expose sensitive customer data if policies or ACLs are incorrect. A concrete case: an S3 bucket containing customer records became publicly accessible because a bucket policy allowed public read; the provider hosts the S3 infrastructure, but the customer configured the policy that exposed the data. Addressing these mistakes is a process you can operationalize. Step one: inventory all public-facing endpoints and storage; step two: enforce account-level defaults that block public bucket creation; step three: run continuous configuration checks with automated tools and remediate findings. Use least privilege for network rules — only allow source IPs or security groups that require access. Misconceptions include thinking that private VPCs automatically protect all attached storage; storage still needs explicit access controls. Practice: run a configuration audit and ask which rules are justified by business needs.

Platform as a Service moves more responsibility to the provider: they manage the operating system, runtime, middleware, and underlying infrastructure. This reduces the customer's duty to patch OS images and manage servers, but it does not remove customer responsibilities entirely. Customers still own application security: secure coding, dependency management, and vulnerability scanning remain critical. Data security is still yours: you must apply encryption, classification, and proper access controls for managed databases or storage. Identity and access management inside the platform must be configured and maintained by the customer, including A P I keys, environment variables, and platform-level roles. A frequent oversight is assuming that because the OS is managed, sensitive data or database users are automatically protected at the application level. For example, a managed database may be patched by the CSP, but you are responsible for strong passwords, least-privilege database users, and encrypting sensitive columns. The right controls combine platform settings and customer-side policies to protect data and access within PaaS offerings. Platform as a Service — what shifts to the CSP means csp manages os/runtime; customer manages app code, database access, data encryption, and iam within the platform.. In practical terms, platform-managed os and runtime, customer-managed code and data.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Software as a Service places the heaviest operational burden on the provider for infrastructure and application maintenance. The CSP manages availability, application patches, server OS, and platform security. Customer responsibilities are narrower but still critical: user identities, access controls, data classification, and application-specific configurations. For instance, migrating email to a SaaS productivity suite makes the provider responsible for service availability and server patching, but the customer must enforce multi-factor authentication, manage user roles, and configure retention and sharing policies for sensitive data. A common pitfall is neglecting strong authentication or granting overly broad permissions inside the SaaS application; a compromised account can still lead to data exfiltration. Data governance remains a customer duty — you must know what data is stored, its sensitivity, and ensure compliance controls like retention and labeling are applied. In short, SaaS reduces infrastructure management but increases the importance of identity controls and data governance inside the application. SaaS — what remains with the customer means csp manages the app stack; customer manages identities, mfa, data classification, governance, and app configuration.. In practical terms, account management, data governance, and configuration inside the application.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Automation is a central technique for meeting customer responsibilities at scale. For patch management, use a systems manager to apply OS updates automatically across instances. For storage, block public access by default at the account level and audit for exceptions. The chapter provides concrete command examples you can run or adapt. The first sample shows how to block public access on an S3 bucket using the provider CLI. The second sample shows how to request a patch run via a systems manager command. These are concrete actions you can automate from CI/CD or runbooks. A misconception is thinking manual fixes are sufficient; automation reduces human error and ensures consistency. Use scheduled scans and playbooks to detect deviations and revert insecure configurations automatically. Below are the exact command examples you may reuse when authorized on your accounts. You must manage user accounts, enforce strong authentication such as multi-factor authentication, and design role-based or attribute-based access control aligned with least privilege. The model requires you to decide who can create resources, who can modify policies, and who can access sensitive data. Concrete practices include using roles for services instead of long-lived credentials, requiring MFA for administrative actions, and regularly reviewing role permissions. Data classification is the first step: know what data you store, its sensitivity, and where it resides. This informs encryption choices, retention policies, and access controls. A common misconception is treating provider-side logs as sufficient; many provider logs show infrastructure events but not tenant-level application accesses. Customers must plan for incidents involving both their own controls and provider-managed elements. An incident response plan should define roles for investigating tenant-level breaches, preserving evidence, and coordinating with the CSP for infrastructure-level problems. For vendor due diligence, validate the provider's certifications, ask for the shared responsibility matrix for services you intend to use, and confirm SLAs and notification procedures for security incidents. Practical questions include: which logs will the provider share, how quickly will they notify you of a platform compromise, and what parts of the stack they will remediate versus you. Now apply what you've learned to a real scenario. Imagine an AWS IaaS deployment where a breached S3 bucket exposed customer data and an unpatched EC2 instance was compromised. Your task is to identify which aspects of the breach are the provider's responsibility and which are the customer's, then propose mitigations for each customer-side failure. For the S3 bucket, responsibility for the bucket policy and ACLs lies with the customer; AWS provides the S3 service but does not set your bucket policies. The mitigation is to block public access at the account or bucket level and audit bucket policies regularly. For the unpatched EC2 OS, the customer owns patching and application hardening; apply automated patch management and vulnerability scanning. Remember these condensed ideas as you work in cloud environments. First, the shared responsibility model divides duties: CSPs secure infrastructure and platforms; customers secure data, OS, applications, and configuration. Second, responsibilities shift with service models: IaaS requires the most customer effort, PaaS reduces OS duties but keeps application and data security with the customer, and SaaS focuses customer duties on identity and data governance. Third, customer responsibilities are measurable and auditable: maintain inventories, automate controls for patching and configuration, enable tenant-level logs, and document ownership in contracts. These concepts are the mental checklist you should use when evaluating a cloud deployment or reviewing an incident. Keep them visible during design and audit conversations to prevent assumptions that lead to security gaps. Carry these three practical rules into your next cloud design review. Rule one: assume responsibility for anything you configure or control inside the tenant — IAM, OS, application, and data. Rule two: automate defensive defaults such as blocking public buckets and enforcing scheduled patching to reduce human error. Rule three: validate vendor claims — request the shared responsibility matrix for each service and map it to your controls and contracts. Together these rules form an operational posture that prevents the majority of common cloud misconfigurations.
